title: Navayana
hook: the "new vehicle" of Ambedkar's followers, centered on justice and equality

segments.voice: Yesterday, Triratna, a new community with an old name. Your line was new community. What small thing did you do to help yours last? Day one thousand three hundred fifty.

Two people pass on a street in Maharashtra, and one says, Jai Bhim. The other says it back. It works as a hello, and it is also a name: Bhim, for Bhimrao Ambedkar. In homes and community halls, his picture hangs beside the Buddha's. Often he is shown in a blue suit and glasses, holding a thick book against his chest. The book is not a sutra. It is a constitution. A Buddhist shrine with a lawyer on it: that pairing is where today begins. Today: Navayana.
screen: `JAI BHIM.` → `A PORTRAIT BESIDE THE BUDDHA.` → `A LAWYER HOLDING A CONSTITUTION.`

segments.voice: First, the man. B. R. Ambedkar was born in India into a community that the caste system treated as untouchable. As a child, he later wrote, he was made to sit apart at school and could not drink from the shared water. He became a lawyer and a scholar, fought caste discrimination, and helped shape the constitution of independent India. Second, the choice. Ambedkar concluded that caste had no place in the path he wanted for his people. After long study he chose the Buddha. And he did not go quietly. At a great public ceremony in the city of Nagpur, he took refuge in the Buddha, the dharma and the sangha, and then led a vast crowd of his followers through the same refuge. He gave them vows that included rejecting caste and treating all people as equal. Third, the teaching. In his book The Buddha and His Dhamma, Ambedkar retold the Buddha's life and words with the weight on ethics and society: liberty, equality, fraternity, and the end of suffering in this life, here, between people. He read some traditional teachings in new ways. Some Buddhists elsewhere disagree with parts of his reading; his followers explain theirs in their own words. The name Navayana means the new vehicle, standing beside the older names for Buddhist paths. Fourth, today. For Dalit Buddhists, those the caste system pushed to the edges, Navayana can be a faith and a dignity at once. Temples hold the Buddha and Ambedkar side by side. Jai Bhim is a greeting, and, for those who say it, also a promise: that the dharma has something to say about who sits where at school, who drinks from which cup, and who gets to be called a person.
screen: `BORN WHERE CASTE SHUT DOORS.` · `A PUBLIC REFUGE IN NAGPUR.` · `THE DHAMMA AS JUSTICE.` · `THE BUDDHA AND AMBEDKAR TOGETHER.` · then, large: `THE NEW VEHICLE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind the people you are likely to see today, one by one: someone you love, someone you work beside, someone who serves you, a stranger on the street. Notice, honestly, whether your mind ranks them, puts some higher and some lower. You don't have to scold the mind for it. Just see it. Then, for each one, silently set them level with yourself, the same height, as if seated around one table. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Navayana. The new vehicle: the Buddhism of B. R. Ambedkar and his followers, centered on justice and the equality of every person. Today's word.

Your line: the new vehicle. Today, treat one person who usually goes unnoticed, a cleaner, a driver, a cashier, exactly as you would treat someone you admire. Use their name if you can. Day one thousand three hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Navayana Buddhists in India, including Dalit communities, take refuge in the Buddha, dharma and sangha, honor B. R. Ambedkar beside the Buddha, greet one another with Jai Bhim, and read the dharma as a call to equality and justice.

original.note: Sanskrit navayana, the new vehicle: the name for the Buddhism of Ambedkar's followers.

trapdoor: what you thought: Ambedkar was a politician, not a religious figure.
what it means: he led his followers into Buddhism as a path of dignity and equality, and his picture stands beside the Buddha's.
what a scholar hears: a reading of the dharma centered on ethics and society, set out in The Buddha and His Dhamma, and named the new vehicle.

sources.ref: the conversion ceremony at Nagpur and the vows given to followers

notes: The year and the size of the Nagpur ceremony and the number of vows are left out under the claims rule ('a vast crowd', 'vows that included').
Childhood details (sitting apart at school, not drinking from shared water) are from Ambedkar's own autobiographical notes; attributed in the voice as 'he later wrote' (Waiting for a Visa); confirm.
'Helped shape the constitution' is deliberately modest; confirm.
The voice says 'caste had no place in the path he wanted' rather than describing the religion he left, to avoid ranking traditions; please have the Hindu path's Keeper also check this framing.
'Some Buddhists elsewhere disagree with parts of his reading' is left general; confirm it is fair to both sides.
Dalit Buddhists described as finding faith and dignity in Navayana ('can be'); confirm framing.
Gloss 'Navayana, the new vehicle' follows the index hook.

Editor: cut the sweeping 'all his life'; 'caste once pushed' became 'the caste system pushed' (so caste is not implied to be over); the closing 'promise' is now framed as the view of those who say Jai Bhim, not the narrator's.
